title: Optical poling of a quantum ferroelectric metal across the order-disorder phase transition
authors: Mohamed Kandil, Yasuhide Tomioka, Yafei Ren, Ryan Comes, Isao H. Inoue, Wencan Jin
abstract: Electron-doped strontium titanate has emerged as a prototypical quantum ferroelectric metal. It provides a fertile ground to explore how ferroelectric instability intertwined with itinerant electrons creates quantum phenomena, including unconventional superconductivity. Despite extensive studies, the microscopic origin of the ferroelectric transition remains unsettled, with distinct interpretations based on displacive mechanism driven by soft mode and order-disorder alignment of local dipoles. In particular, the local dipoles form nanoscale, spatially heterogeneous clusters, termed polar nanoregions, posing a significant challenge for probing or manipulating them. Here, using rotational anisotropy second harmonic generation, a symmetry-resolved probe, we quantify the orientational statistics of polar nanoregions in dilute electron-doped Sr$_{0.95}$Ba$_{0.05}$Ti$_{1-x}$Nb$_x$O$_3$. By tracking the alignment and meltdown of polar nanoregions in thermal cycles, we unambiguously demonstrate the order-disorder nature of the ferroelectric transition. We further show that, above transition temperature, femtosecond optical fields enable deterministic control of otherwise disordered polar nanoregions, realizing reversible write and readout of polar textures on ultrafast timescales. Our findings provide new insight into ferroelectric instability and establish an all-optical route of controlling polar metal systems where conventional electrical approaches are not feasible.
summary: This work investigates the ferroelectric transition in quantum ferroelectric metals using advanced optical techniques. By employing RA-SHG and pump-probe measurements, the authors confirm the order-disorder nature of the transition. Crucially, they demonstrate that femtosecond optical pulses can deterministically align the disordered polar nanoregions, opening an all-optical pathway for controlling these quantum materials.
main_problem: The paper addresses the unsettled microscopic origin of the ferroelectric transition in quantum ferroelectric metals and seeks to develop methods to probe and control the associated polar nanoregions.
main_result: The study unambiguously demonstrates the order-disorder nature of the ferroelectric transition and establishes an all-optical route to deterministically control the orientation of these polar nanoregions.
method: The research combines symmetry-resolved optical measurements (Rotational Anisotropy Second Harmonic Generation, RA-SHG) with ultrafast pump-probe spectroscopy to track polarization dynamics.
model_or_system: The physical system is electron-doped strontium titanate, a prototypical quantum ferroelectric metal. The analysis models the local dipoles as tunneling between states, and the SHG response is analyzed based on fluctuations in local polarization ($\langle P^2 angle$-type).
key_observables: RA-SHG intensity patterns, which reveal orientational statistics; the divergence of $\Delta I_{	ext{SHG}}$ near the transition temperature ($T_{	ext{FE}}$); and the degree of alignment achieved via optical poling.
important_parameters: Temperature ($T$), carrier concentration, and the polarization angle ($\delta$) of the incident optical pump field.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the SHG signal is dominated by local dipole fluctuations and that the optical poling process can be modeled by fitting the pump-probe signal to a specific functional form.
figures_summary: Figures show temperature-dependent phase diagrams, RA-SHG patterns confirming 2-fold symmetry, and pump-probe measurements demonstrating that the optical field aligns over 80% of the polar nanoregions above the transition temperature.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical system and the debate between ferroelectric mechanisms. It then uses RA-SHG to characterize the transition as order-disorder. Finally, it employs pump-probe spectroscopy to demonstrate deterministic, ultrafast optical control (poling) of the polar nanoregions.
why_interesting: The ability to use light to deterministically write and read out polarization textures in a quantum material provides a novel, non-electrical control mechanism, which is highly relevant for understanding and manipulating quantum states in condensed matter systems.
